newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Heroin smuggled from China seized in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Heroin smuggled from China seized in Taiwan.

text.p: Police on Thursday seized 8.8 kg (19 pounds) of heroin and arrested two Taiwan men on charges of spiriting the drugs in from China, possibly for a major Hong Kong smuggling syndicate, officials said.
Narcotics police involved in the arrest of Wu Chi-yi and Liu Jung-jun said they had evidence they had smuggled the heroin from southern China by boat, state-run television reported.
Authorities said the 8.8 kgs of heroin had a value of more than T$100 million (US$3.64 million) but said that paled in comparison to the potential social harm.
"The severity of the damage these drugs would do to our people if released into the market is hard to imagine," said Wang Jung-chou, head of Taiwan's investigation bureau.
Bureau detectives suspected an international drug ring based in Hong Kong had organised the shipment and may be involved in widespread drug trafficking in the region.

"We can be sure that these drugs were smuggled from the (Chinese) mainland by fishing boats to southern Taiwan and were scheduled to be distributed throughout the Taiwan region," said another bureau official, Wang Hua-fu.
The bureau said it hoped to cooperate with China, Taiwan's diplomatic rival since a civil war split them in 1949, to curb drug trafficking across the Taiwan strait.
Semi-official bilateral talks have been on hold since what had been warming ties were frozen in mid-1995 in the latest political rift between Beijing and Taipei.
Taiwan has seen drug use rise during a social and political renaissance that followed the lifting of martial law in 1987.
Likewise, China largely eliminated the nationwide scourge of opium after the 1949 communist takeover but has seen drug use return during two decades of reform-driven prosperity.

Beijing generally blames China's growing drug problem on smugglers from Taiwan, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia's opium-growing Golden Triangle who have exploited China's porous borders to blaze new transshipment trails.
